title: Working backwards through two steps
objectives: Price an option on a two-step tree by backward induction.
Check a two-step price with the binomial formula and with put-call parity.

screens.title: Two years, four paths
screens.prose: The share from level 1 starts at £100. Each year its price is multiplied by $u = 1.2$ or by $d = 0.8$. Now it moves twice.

state.caption: Each year the price is multiplied by 1.2 or by 0.8

screens.question: Tap the two paths that end at the same price.

hints.text: Multiply £100 by the two factors along each path.
Look at the two middle paths: up then down, and down then up.
$100 \times 1.2 \times 0.8 = 96$ and $100 \times 0.8 \times 1.2 = 96$. The order of the factors does not matter.

feedback.correct: Up then down and down then up both end at £96.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the price at the end of each path, then find the two that match.

byKey.u-u: Up twice gives £144. No other path reaches that price.
byKey.d-d: Down twice gives £64. No other path reaches that price.
byKey.u-d: Up then down is one of them. Find the other path that ends at £96.
byKey.d-u: Down then up is one of them. Find the other path that ends at £96.

explain.text: Multiplying by 1.2 then 0.8 gives the same as 0.8 then 1.2: £96. So the tree **recombines**. Two steps give three prices, £144, £96 and £64, not four.

screens.title: What the call pays
screens.prose: We redraw the tree with the two middle paths joined into one node. A European call struck at £100 expires at year 2.

state.caption: Each node shows the share price; the call’s value goes underneath

screens.question: Fill in the call’s payoff at each year-2 node.

hints.text: A call pays the share price minus the strike, when that is positive.
At £96 the share is below the strike.
$\max(144 - 100, 0) = 44$. The other two prices are below £100.

feedback.correct: £44 at the top and nothing at the other two.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each payoff is $\max(S - 100, 0)$.

byKey.r1c1: At £96 the call is out of the money. $96 - 100$ is negative, so it pays nothing.
byKey.r2c1: At £64 the share is far below the strike, so the call pays nothing.

explain.text: Only the top node pays: £44. A call’s payoff at expiry is $\max(S - K, 0)$. Now we need its value today, two steps away.

screens.title: The last step is one step
screens.prose: Stand at the £120 node. One step remains, to £144 or £96. That is a one-step tree like level 1’s, with $q = 0.625$ and $r = 5\%$.

state.caption: From £120: up to £144, or down to £96

screens.question: What is the call worth at the £120 node?

hints.text: Weight the two payoffs by $q$ and $1 - q$, then discount one step.
Up pays £44 and down pays £0.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight £44 and £0 by $q$ and $1 - q$, then divide by 1.05.

byKey.no-disc: You weighted the payoffs but did not discount. The £27.50 arrives a year later, so divide by 1.05.
byKey.no-q: You discounted £44 as if it were certain. It comes only in the up state, with weight 0.625.
byKey.half: You used equal weights. The risk-neutral weight on up is $q = 0.625$, from level 1.
byKey.intrinsic: £20 is what $120 - 100$ would pay now. A European call cannot be exercised before year 2.

explain.text: You priced a one-step tree inside the bigger one: £26.19 at the £120 node. Working from the last step back to today is **backward induction**. Each node’s value comes from the two nodes after it.

screens.title: Back to today
screens.prose: The £80 node leads to £96 and £64, where the call pays nothing. The £120 node is now worth £26.19. Use the same rule twice more.

state.caption: Values so far: the year-2 payoffs and the £120 node

screens.question: Fill in the call’s value at the £80 node and today.

hints.text: Each node uses the two nodes one step after it.
Today’s two next nodes are £120 and £80.
£80 node: both next values are 0. Today: $\dfrac{0.625 \times 26.19 + 0.375 \times 0}{1.05}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight the two next values by 0.625 and 0.375, then divide by 1.05.

byKey.r0c1: Both nodes after £80 pay nothing, so the call is worth nothing there.
byKey.r1c1: Today’s value weights £26.19 by 0.625 and discounts once more by 1.05. Each step back costs one discount.

explain.text: Two backward steps give £15.59 today: $0.625 \times 26.19 / 1.05$. Each step weights by $q$ and $1 - q$ and discounts once. Two steps mean two discounts.

screens.title: One discount for two years
screens.prose: A colleague skips the middle nodes. The call pays £44 only after two ups, with weight $q^2 = 0.390625$. She computes $44 \times 0.390625 / 1.05$.

state.caption: The only paying path: up, then up again

screens.question: What is the call worth today?

options.why: You discounted once. The £44 arrives two years away, so divide by $1.05^2$.
You priced off year 1, where £120 pays £20. The call runs to year 2, so start from its year-2 payoffs.
That is $44 \times q^2$ with no discount at all. Money in two years is worth less today.

hints.text: How many years away is the £44?
Each step back divides by 1.05.
$44 \times 0.390625 / 1.05^2 = 15.59$, the same as backward induction.

feedback.correct: The weight $q^2$ is right; the discount must be $1.05^2$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the discounts: one for each year between the payoff and today.

byKey.once: You discounted once. The £44 arrives two years away, so divide by $1.05^2$.
byKey.forwards: You priced off year 1, where £120 pays £20. The call runs to year 2, so start from its year-2 payoffs.

explain.text: Her weight $q^2$ is right: two ups in a row. But £44 paid in two years needs two discounts: $17.1875 / 1.1025 = 15.59$. That matches backward induction exactly.

screens.title: The two-step formula
screens.prose: Write $C_{uu}, C_{ud}, C_{dd}$ for the year-2 payoffs and $R = 1.05$. Turn backward induction into one formula.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $C_u = \dfrac{qC_{uu} + (1-q)C_{ud}}{R}$ and $C_d = \dfrac{qC_{ud} + (1-q)C_{dd}}{R}$: one step back from year 2
$C_0 = \dfrac{qC_u + (1-q)C_d}{R}$: one more step back, to today
$C_0 = \dfrac{q^2C_{uu} + 2q(1-q)C_{ud} + (1-q)^2C_{dd}}{R^2}$: substitute, and collect the middle node’s two paths

hints.text: Start where backward induction starts: at year 1.
Substituting needs both year-1 values, so it comes after them.
Year-1 values, then today’s value, then substitute, then write the weights as $\binom{2}{k}$.

feedback.correct: Two steps back, then substitute and collect.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow backward induction first, then simplify.

byKey.c: The substitution needs $C_u$ and $C_d$ and today’s formula first.
byKey.d: The sum is a compact way to write the collected line, so it comes last.

explain.text: The middle node is reached by two paths, so its weight is $2q(1-q)$: that is $\binom{2}{1}$. The weights are binomial probabilities, and the discount is $R^2$. For the call only $k = 2$ pays: $0.390625 \times 44 / 1.1025 = 15.59$.

screens.title: A put on the same tree
screens.prose: Now a European put struck at £100, on the same tree. It pays $\max(100 - S, 0)$ at year 2: £0, £4 and £36.
screens.question: Use the two-step formula. What is the put worth today?

hints.text: Which nodes pay, and how many paths reach each one?
The £96 node pays £4 and has two paths. The £64 node pays £36 and has one.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each payoff by $\binom{2}{k}q^k(1-q)^{2-k}$, then divide by $1.05^2$.

byKey.no-two: You gave the £96 node one path. Up-down and down-up both reach it, so its weight is $2q(1-q)$.
byKey.no-disc: You weighted correctly but did not discount. Divide by $1.05^2$.
byKey.once: You discounted once. The payoffs are two years away, so divide by $1.05^2$.

explain.text: The £96 node adds $1.875$ and the £64 node $5.0625$; over $1.1025$ that is £6.29. Put-call parity checks it: $C - P = 15.59 - 6.29 = 9.30$. And $S_0 - K/1.05^2 = 100 - 90.70 = 9.30$.

screens.title: A strike that never pays
screens.prose: Move the strike. Every node’s call value updates by backward induction.
screens.question: What is the smallest strike at which the call is worth nothing at every node?

widget.label: Smallest strike, in £
widget.accept: £144: at or above it, no year-2 node pays.

hints.text: Slide the strike up and watch the top node.
Once the strike passes £96, only the £144 node can pay.

feedback.correct: At $K = 144$ every payoff, and so every value, is zero.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find where the top node’s payoff reaches zero.

byKey.year1: At $K = 120$ the £144 node still pays £24, so the call has value.
byKey.start: At £100 the top node pays £44. Raise the strike further.
byKey.middle: Above £96 the middle node stops paying, but the £144 node still pays.

explain.text: At $K = 144$ no year-2 node pays, so every value back to today is £0. A payoff that is zero at every leaf is worth nothing, whatever $q$ is. Just below £144, the top node keeps a little value alive.

screens.title: The hedge moves
screens.prose: In level 1 the hedge held $\Delta = \dfrac{C_{\text{up}} - C_{\text{down}}}{S_{\text{up}} - S_{\text{down}}}$ shares. On a two-step tree each node starts its own one-step tree, so it has its own delta.
screens.question: Fill in the call’s delta at each node, to 2 decimal places.

hints.text: At each node, divide the change in the call by the change in the share over the next step.
From £120 the share goes to £144 or £96, and the call to £44 or £0.

feedback.correct: 0.65 today, 0.92 after an up move, 0 after a down move.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the two nodes one step after each node.

byKey.r0c1: Today’s next nodes are £120 and £80, worth £26.19 and £0: $26.19 / 40 = 0.65$.
byKey.r1c1: From £120 the call goes to £44 or £0 while the share goes to £144 or £96: $44 / 48$.
byKey.r2c1: From £80 the call is worth £0 in both states, so the hedge needs no shares.

explain.text: Delta is 0.65 today, 0.92 after an up move and 0 after a down move. So the hedge must be rebalanced at year 1. Level 3 turns this rebalancing into a strategy: delta hedging.

screens.title: A bond that can default twice
screens.prose: A two-year corporate bond repays £100 at year 2. Each year the firm defaults with risk-neutral probability 4%. On default, holders get £40 at the end of that year. The risk-free rate is 5%.

state.caption: Risk-neutral chances; default pays £40 at the end of that year

screens.question: What is the bond worth today?

widget.label: Bond value today, in £
widget.accept: £86.51: £92.95 at the year-1 survival node, then $(0.96 \times 92.95 + 0.04 \times 40)/1.05$.

hints.text: Start at the year-1 survival node. What is the bond worth there?
From there it pays £100 or £40 one year later.

feedback.correct: £92.95 after one year of survival, £86.51 today.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Value the year-1 survival node first, then step back to today.

byKey.riskfree: £90.70 is $100/1.05^2$, a bond that never defaults. Default risk must lower the price.
byKey.once: You discounted two years of payments by 1.05 only once. Each step back needs its own discount.
byKey.late: You discounted the year-1 recovery for two years. It is paid at year 1, so it needs one discount.
byKey.no-recovery: You left out the £40 recovery. Holders get it if the firm defaults.

explain.text: Backward induction gives £92.95 at the survival node and £86.51 today. A risk-free bond would be worth £90.70, so £4.19 is the price of default risk. This tree does not recombine, because default ends the bond.

ideas: Up then down equals down then up, so an $n$-step tree has only $n + 1$ final prices.
Backward induction: each node is worth $\dfrac{qV_{\text{up}} + (1-q)V_{\text{down}}}{1 + r}$, from expiry back to today.
The binomial formula gives the same price, with one discount for each step.

formula.name: Two-step price
formula.note: The middle node has two paths. Weight by $q$, never by the real chance of up.

summary.trap: £44 paid in two years needs two discounts: £15.59, not £16.37.

quiz.prose: On the two-step tree ($S_0 = 100$, $u = 1.2$, $d = 0.8$, $r = 5\%$ a year) a European call and put are both struck at £100.
quiz.question: What is the call price minus the put price?

options.why: You assumed a call and put struck at the same price are worth the same. Parity says $C - P = S_0 - K/(1 + r)^2$.
That is $100 - 100/1.05$, one year of discounting. Both options run two years.
That is the call alone. Subtract the put’s £6.29.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use put-call parity over two years.

explain.text: Parity gives $C - P = S_0 - K/(1 + r)^2 = 100 - 90.70 = 9.30$. The tree agrees: $15.59 - 6.29 = 9.30$. Parity holds node by node, so it holds on any tree.

quiz.prose: A one-year tree has 12 monthly steps, and it recombines.
quiz.question: How many different share prices are possible at the end of the year?

feedback.correct: One final price for each number of ups, 0 to 12.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A final price depends only on how many of the 12 steps went up.

byKey.paths: 4,096 is $2^{12}$, the number of paths. Paths with the same number of ups end at the same price.
byKey.steps: Count 0 ups as well: 0 to 12 is 13 values.
byKey.double: A recombining tree adds one price per step, not two.

explain.text: A final price is $S_0u^kd^{12-k}$, set by the number of ups $k$ from 0 to 12. So there are 13 prices. More steps give a finer grid of final prices.

quiz.question: What is it worth today?
